n1a.why: One market, one product category and two decision-makers is a standard 6-9 week entry assessment, so X's 4-5 week Research fits while Y's 5-7 weeks pads it, although Y's note that a no-go ends the work after Research is the more useful gate for pricing.

n1b.why: Four markets plus sequencing fits in 10-14 weeks if a desk screen narrows the field, and Y is the only plan that states that assumption, its effect on weeks, and the risk that a desk-only no-go may not meet the per-country go/no-go criterion, while X's notes give the partner nothing to confirm.

n2a.why: One plant with three lines needs about 3-5 weeks of diagnostic and 8-12 weeks for improvements to show up in cost per part, which matches X, while Y's 12-14 week Implementation is padded for a site this size and its notes do not say what drives it.

n2b.why: Six plants in two countries with 19 lines need a pilot plant and then rollout waves before cost per part moves in every plant, so X's 14-16 week Implementation is squeezed, while Y's 25-29 weeks follows from a stated pilot and wave sizing and flags the open choice of which three plants to diagnose on the floor.

n3a.why: A 140-person claims department redesign normally reaches executive committee approval in 8-12 weeks, so Y's 10-12 week Design is padded, but X's single note does not tell the partner what to confirm, and Y wrongly calls the headcount public research when the brief gives it.

n3b.why: A target operating model and transition plan for five units and 1,800 people across 14 locations is typically 16-20 weeks, so X's 14-week low end is slightly tight and Y's 22-26 weeks, with a 9-11 week Diagnostic, is hard to justify to a CFO, and neither set of notes names what drives the length beyond the unit count.

n4a.why: Requirements, vendor choice and a configured, piloted rollout to 40 pharmacies at 5-8 stores a week fit in 22-30 weeks, so X is about right (its 14-16 week Implementation is lean if it must cover configuration and a pilot) and Y's 25-27 week Implementation is long, although Y's tender caveat is the most useful note on either plan.

n4b.why: Selecting an ERP and taking three modules live, with data migration, across 42 sites usually means 8-12 weeks of selection and 6-9 months of implementation, so X's 22-24 weeks leaves no room for testing or a pilot, while Y is closer and its notes name the drivers (weeks per area, wave length, tender) that would move it.

n5.why: A digital channels strategy for one bank is usually 8-12 weeks, so Y's 16-22 weeks is padded, but neither plan flags the missing success criteria, which is the biggest sizing risk, and only Y names the assumed channel and segment counts to confirm.

n6.why: A board-ready plan for three companies fits in the 12 weeks, but moving one company's sales, purchasing and finance onto new processes and systems does not fit in 3-5 weeks, and only X says the work sizes at 19-28 weeks and flags that cutover would start before the board approves the plan.
